claims.text: The homogenized starting alloy has a dual-phase FCC/B2 lamellar structure.
The starting alloy is strong but brittle because its incoherent interfaces are susceptible to interfacial cracking.
Room-temperature brittleness and limited ductility in conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys arise from incoherent interfaces and pronounced dislocation pile-ups.

Treating Al0.7CoCrFeNi at 6 GPa and 1473 K for 2 hours in a hexahedron-anvil apparatus, followed by controlled cooling and decompression, will transform its lamellar structure into a hierarchical microstructure.
The HPHT-induced hierarchical microstructure will contain coherent interfaces between FCC and B2 phases.
Coherent FCC/B2 interfaces will facilitate preferential dislocation transfer.
Improved dislocation transfer across FCC/B2 interfaces will reduce dislocation pile-ups and associated local stress concentrations.
The HPHT-generated hierarchical microstructure will activate dislocations, stacking faults, microbands, and twins as multiple deformation modes.
Activation of multiple deformation modes will produce a more homogeneous strain distribution.
The HPHT-treated alloy will reach a strength of approximately 1150 MPa.
The HPHT-treated alloy will reach tensile ductility of approximately 36%.
HPHT treatment will simultaneously increase strength and tensile ductility relative to the untreated starting material.
HPHT treatment will change fracture behavior from catastrophic interfacial cracking to distributed microcracking.
Achieving the proposed improvement requires the specific combination of 6 GPa and 1473 K.
Lower-pressure treatments and conventional hot isostatic pressing will not produce comparable improvements.
EBSD can be used to verify reduced dislocation pile-ups and FCC/B2 interface coherence in this experiment.
